title: Desktop Spelling List Editor & Program Generator

contributors.contribution: Provided consulting assistance while Jamie designed and implemented the desktop Spelling List Editor.

description: I designed and built the desktop Spelling List Editor, a customer-facing Java/Swing authoring tool that let teachers create complete Essential Skills spelling programs without programming. Teachers built recursive menu trees of spelling lists, entered their own words, recorded each word with a microphone, and the tool automatically generated the formatted activity content and inserted it into the shared ISAM database. The resulting teacher-created program behaved like a native ESS program in both the student software and Marks Manager / Teacher Dashboard.

sections.title: More Than a Spelling List Editor
paragraphs: Although the product was called Spelling List Editor, it effectively generated complete mini spelling programs.
Teachers could build hierarchical menus, add word lists anywhere in the tree, record audio for each word, and automatically receive a complete set of student activities.

sections.title: Recursive Program Structure
paragraphs: The authoring model used a true recursive menu structure stored in the Essential Skills ISAM content database.
A teacher could create menus inside menus and place word lists at any level, allowing a custom program to be organized by week, unit, topic, grade, teacher preference, or any other structure.

sections.title: Simple Teacher Workflow
paragraphs: Teachers did not need to understand the internal Essential Skills activity format.
They created the menu structure, entered a list of spelling words, and then used a recording wizard to capture the pronunciation for each word.
items: Record each word through the microphone wizard

sections.title: Automatic Lesson Generation
paragraphs: The tool converted the teacher's small amount of authored input into fully formatted Essential Skills lesson data.
It generated the spelling activities automatically and inserted them directly into the ISAM content database.

sections.title: 11 Core Activity Families
paragraphs: Surviving screenshots from the later Version 7 port document 11 core spelling activity families generated from the teacher's word lists.
Several activity families also had alternate or randomized interaction variants, so repeated play could present a different version of the same activity.

sections.title: Activity Variety
paragraphs: The generated program was not a single repeated quiz format.

The activity set used different mechanics including listening, recognition, memory matching, typing, word shapes, letter reconstruction, missing-letter completion, flash-card study, and spelling from audio.

sections.title: Randomized Variants
paragraphs: Some activities included alternate or randomized presentation modes.
This meant students could revisit the same teacher-created list without always receiving the exact same screen or interaction pattern.

sections.title: Microphone Recording Wizard
paragraphs: Teachers recorded only the spelling word itself.
The wizard walked through the word list one item at a time, allowing the teacher to record and then play back each pronunciation before continuing.

sections.title: Custom WAV Recording
paragraphs: I implemented the audio-recording path in JNI/C++ rather than relying on a high-level Java recording abstraction.
I wrote the WAV output logic from scratch, including creating the file header, streaming sample data, closing the recording, calculating final sizes, and updating the required WAV header fields.

sections.title: Cross-Platform Audio Access
paragraphs: The application had to support both Windows and Mac teacher workstations.
QuickTime and native media APIs provided access to the microphone hardware, while JNI connected the Java/Swing application to the native recording implementation.

sections.title: Native ESS Program Compatibility
paragraphs: Teacher-created content was not stored as a separate toy format.
The Spelling List Editor generated a real Essential Skills program structure inside the same content system used by production software.

sections.title: Student Experience
paragraphs: Students saw teacher-created menus and activities through the normal Essential Skills student application.
They navigated the recursive menus just as they would navigate a professionally produced ESS program and reached the generated spelling activities at the end of the menu path.

sections.title: Marks Manager / Teacher Dashboard Integration
paragraphs: Because the generated content conformed to the standard Essential Skills program architecture, it plugged into the normal Marks Manager / Teacher Dashboard workflow.
Teacher-created spelling programs could therefore participate in the same classroom-management and reporting ecosystem as standard ESS programs.

sections.title: Shared Local / Network Database
paragraphs: The custom spelling program lived inside the Essential Skills ISAM database on either the local machine or the school's shared file server.
This matched the deployment model used by the broader desktop Essential Skills suite.

sections.title: Customer Product
paragraphs: The Spelling List Editor was sold separately to customers rather than being only an internal authoring utility.
It was sufficiently used in schools that microphone configuration became a recurring technical-support issue, commonly involving muted microphones or incorrectly configured system input devices.

sections.title: Version 3 Era
paragraphs: The Spelling List Editor was built after Version 2 and is best associated with the Version 3 / mid-2000s desktop generation.
It remained compatible with later Hydra-Gen-era desktop software but was not rebuilt for the Java WebStart transition.

sections.title: End of the Desktop Generation
paragraphs: The original desktop editor did not carry directly into Version 6 because the HTML5 platform and content architecture were fundamentally different.
Later web-era spelling authoring systems therefore represented a new implementation rather than a straightforward continuation of the old Java tool.

sections.title: Later Activity Preservation
paragraphs: The original spelling activities were important enough that screenshots of the desktop-era activity set were later retained as reference material when the activities were recreated for Version 7.

historicalNotes: The product's original customer-facing name was Spelling List Editor.
The portfolio title expands the name because the tool created complete mini spelling programs rather than merely editing flat word lists.
The tool was built after Version 2 and is most likely a Version 3 / mid-2000s product.
The public date range 2004-2006 is a working estimate and should be revised if stronger source evidence is recovered.
Teachers could create a true recursive menu tree in the ISAM database.
Menus could contain submenus recursively, with spelling word lists placed at any level.
Teachers entered only a list of words and recorded the pronunciation of each word.
Audio recordings contained the word only, not sentences or definitions.
A recording wizard stepped through the list and allowed playback of recorded words.
Jamie implemented WAV recording twice in JNI/C++ from scratch, including WAV header creation, data streaming, final size calculation, and header updates.
QuickTime and native media APIs were used to gain microphone hardware access on Mac and PC.
Jamie remembers media.dll as likely Microsoft-provided; exact ownership/API identity should remain low confidence unless source code is recovered.
The tool generated all required lesson/activity data and inserted it directly into the Essential Skills ISAM content database.
The database could live locally or on a remote/shared school file server.
The generated spelling program was fully compatible with the standard Essential Skills student application and Marks Manager / Teacher Dashboard.
Students saw the teacher-authored menus and activities like any regular Essential Skills program.
The product was sold separately to customers.
Frequent microphone support issues are remembered as evidence of substantial real-world use, but this should be treated as circumstantial rather than a quantified adoption metric.
Jamie built the product primarily himself with some assistance from the original Version 1 creator acting as a consultant.
The tool remained compatible through the Hydra-Gen desktop era but was not adapted to Java WebStart.
It could not be carried directly into Version 6 because the HTML5 platform represented a fundamentally different architecture.
Surviving screenshots from the later Version 7 recreation document the activity set.
The screenshots are stronger evidence than Jamie's initial rough memory of 10 activities.
The screenshot inventory supports 11 core activity families, with some families showing alternate or randomized interaction variants.
Do not claim there were only 11 total possible screens because randomized/alternate modes could produce additional presentations.
The four supporting screenshots selected for the public card should represent distinct activity mechanics rather than near-duplicate variants.
